GeoGPT geology workshop · Keep this lesson open

Where should a team look for earthquake landslides?

After the Gorkha earthquake in Nepal, a response team would need to decide where to look for landslides. Steep ground and strong shaking both matter. You will give GeoGPT the numbers behind a terrain map, the USGS shaking map and a fixed model. It will calculate a map showing where that model assigns higher relative landslide occurrence.

What you will learn

Combine two kinds of map evidence and distinguish a model prediction from an observed landslide.

The computer task: one supplied data file and one prompt.

The lesson supplies every setting. You do not have to invent a question, read a paper or write code.

Four words, explained here

Terrain
The shape of the ground, including how steep the slopes are.

Shaking
Ground acceleration during the earthquake. PGA means the strongest acceleration.

Model
A supplied mathematical rule that combines terrain and shaking.

Relative score
Higher means a stronger modeled tendency compared with lower scores. It is not a confirmed landslide or a measured chance of failure.

A prompt is an instruction to GeoGPT. This button copies the entire instruction; you do not need to read its technical settings or edit anything.

Show the words this button copies — no editing needed
Complete this beginner teaching task in English using the uploaded gorkha-inputs.csv. It contains archived terrain and USGS Gorkha mainshock shaking, already matched by location to reduce file handling. No predicted scores or landslide labels are supplied. If this input is missing or unreadable, name it and stop; otherwise execute without asking for settings, validation, thresholds or permission. Check 6920 unique cell_id rows. Coordinates x_m,y_m are EPSG:32645 metres; each cell is a 500 m square. Terrain elevation_mean_m is map context; slope_mean_deg and relief_m are predictors. Shaking pga_pctg is percent g, so do not divide it by 100. Apply the instructor-fitted model exactly: z=-11.890769756601834+0.24531040883053476*slope_mean_deg-0.0061609749185370013*relief_m+0.091060379532196728*pga_pctg; score=1/(1+exp(-z)). Do not retrain or request an inventory. This model was fitted beforehand on 20203 southern cells; these are 6920 northern cells. It is not the USGS published global model and scores are not calibrated probabilities. Execute and save potential-landslides.csv with cell_id, coordinates and score; potential_landslides.py; potential-landslides.png. Plot three vertically stacked maps on a 12 by 16 inch canvas: Terrain (elevation); Shaking (PGA); Relative occurrence (score). Use the same extent, equal spatial aspect, north up, easting/northing in kilometres, at most five ticks per axis, separate readable colorbars. Score scale 0..1 labelled “Relative landslide-occurrence score (not calibrated probability)”. The supplied cells cover an irregular subset of the map rectangle. Leave all other locations blank; do not fill or interpolate them. Include this caption: “Blank areas are outside the supplied cells: no prediction.” Check the count of populated cells rather than claiming complete geographic coverage. Inspect the actual figure for readable labels. Report filenames, unique-cell count and min/mean/max score, then four short ordinary-language sentences: identify the highest-scoring cell by its plotted easting and northing in kilometres, read directly from the computed CSV; explain what a higher relative score means for choosing where to inspect; state one limitation; explain that blank patches mean no supplied prediction, not safety. Do not guess compass-direction clusters, ridges, valleys or causal spatial patterns. Do not invent slope aspect, lithology, groundwater, confirmed failures or runout. Source shaking: USGS event us20002926; source terrain: archived Skadi SRTM-based compilation with fills. Not present-day measurements. No fabricated results. End with “Finished. Return to the lesson.” Do not ask another question.

Next: Understand the result ↓

Understand the result, one point at a time

The single file contains terrain measurements and USGS earthquake acceleration at matching locations. These were combined beforehand to save upload steps; no prediction is in that input. The prompt supplies the fixed rule. Download and upload the file without editing it. These are archived Gorkha data, not present-day measurements. No training, fitting, threshold choice or landslide inventory is required.

Read the legend beside each map.

The legend is the strip that explains the colors. Each map shows a different quantity. A similar color on two maps does not mean the same number.

Compare one place across all three maps.

Use the same horizontal and vertical map position each time. Find a higher-score place and a lower-score place. Terrain and shaking jointly contribute to the score.

Separate prediction from observation.

A higher score suggests a place to check. It does not establish that a landslide happened. A blank cell means missing supplied coverage, not safety.

A tempting claim to check

“A high score means that location definitely failed.” It is a modeled priority for checking. Material strength, water conditions and how debris travels are not resolved by this map.

Talk it through

Use your own result. Speak to a partner or think quietly; you do not have to type an answer.

  1. Choose one higher-score area. What would you inspect there?
  2. What does a blank patch mean? What would be wrong with calling it safe?
  3. What additional image or field observation would establish whether a landslide actually occurred?
After discussing: read an example explanation

A useful result is a relative-occurrence map plus a cautious explanation of where to look. Satellite images or field observations are needed to confirm failures. The 0–1 score is not a locally calibrated probability and is not a calculation of forces resisting failure.

Optional: try one idea

The required investigation is already complete. If you have time, use this suggestion or explain an idea of your own before trying it.

Ask GeoGPT: “Use the existing computed map and values. Describe one higher-score area and one lower-score area using the plotted coordinates. Do not invent slope direction, geology or confirmed failures. Explain one limitation in plain language.”

Your 45-minute class guide

The computer run is short. Take the class time to learn the controls, inspect evidence and explain your reasoning. These are gentle reminders, not a deadline.

Class minutesWhere to be
0–10Read the question and four words. Open GeoGPT and prepare the inputs.
10–15Send the one prompt and open its result.
15–25Follow the three points under Understand the result. Locate the evidence yourself.
25–35Discuss the questions and check the tempting claim.
35–45Explore one idea, compare explanations and ask questions.
Optional research background and sources

Rapid regional earthquake-landslide assessment is an active application. This example uses an instructor-fitted equation and archived terrain and shaking. It illustrates the combination of evidence, not the full USGS global model or an operational safety assessment.
